h1: Build out, build up, build once
hero_sub: Rear extensions, second stories, garage and terrace conversions, and in-law suites across Miami-Dade and Broward. Engineered before they are drawn, permitted in the right jurisdiction, and supervised on site every working day by a licensed general contractor. Lic. CGC1539072.
intro_paragraphs: A home addition at this level is not a bonus room. It is a rear extension that finally gives a 1958 house the kitchen and family room it was never drawn with, a second story over a lot that is already full, a garage or screened terrace turned into real conditioned space, or a suite for parents who now spend half the year here. People who build an addition are rarely short of options. They already have the street, the school, the dock or the tree canopy they wanted, and moving would cost more than building.

What changes here sits under the finishes. Miami-Dade and Broward together are Florida's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ), so every new window, door and roof assembly needs an approval valid there, backed by large-missile impact and pressure-cycling testing. Near saltwater the code stops treating corrosion as a finish question, which is why coastal connectors and anchors get detailed in stainless. In a flood zone, crossing FEMA's substantial-improvement threshold pulls the entire structure into compliance, not just the new part. The two counties are not one market: each layers a county Board of Rules and Appeals over its municipal building departments, with its own code amendments and certified inspectors, and Miami-Dade spreads across thirty-four municipalities plus a large unincorporated county.

An addition can be priced honestly only after it has been engineered. So we start with a survey, a structural evaluation and a hard look at setbacks, easements and flood data, before anyone puts a number on a finish. What you sign is a fixed written scope: the work, the allowances, the sequence, and the inspections it has to pass. A supervisor is on site every working day, the occupied half of the house stays sealed and livable, and the permit is closed out rather than left open for a future buyer's title search to discover. One accountable team, from estimate through warranty.

The same service looks different from one end of this market to the other. In Coral Gables and Miami Beach, an addition has to satisfy design review before an engineer ever sizes a footing. On the Broward waterfront, in Rio Vista, Harbor Beach, Las Olas Isles and Lighthouse Point, elevation and what the county allows near the water decide the footprint. In Weston, Parkland and Southwest Ranches, the platted envelope, the drainage easement and the septic system decide it instead. We build additions in forty-two areas across both counties. Each has a page of its own here, with the local rules spelled out. Find yours.
scope_heading: Six ways a South Florida house grows
scope_intro: Every one of these begins with an engineer and a survey, not a mood board. These are the shapes additions actually take across the two counties.

scope_items.name: Rear and side extensions
scope_items.desc: New living space pushed into the yard for kitchens, family rooms and primary suites, with foundations, tie beams and the roof joint engineered and permitted as one package.

scope_items.name: Second stories and over-garage floors
scope_items.desc: Upper floors where existing footings, block walls and tie beams carry the load, with reinforcement, new columns or an upgraded beam designed in wherever the numbers say otherwise.

scope_items.name: Garage and terrace conversions
scope_items.desc: Covered, screened or unconditioned space converted into permitted living area with impact openings, insulation, mechanical capacity and an engineered roof, so the new square footage is real, permitted and defensible when an appraiser asks.

scope_items.name: In-law and guest suites
scope_items.desc: Independent quarters with bath, closet and kitchenette for parents, adult children or long-staying guests, proportioned to belong to the house rather than lean against it.

scope_items.name: Foundations, tie beams, structural tie-ins
scope_items.desc: New footings, underpinning where the soil asks for it, reinforced tie beams and truss work, joined to the existing structure the way the engineer drew it and not the way that moves fastest.

scope_items.name: Permits, approvals and inspections
scope_items.desc: Plan sets filed in the correct jurisdiction, HVHZ product approvals assembled, zoning and flood questions settled up front, phased inspections passed, and the permit closed at the end.

faqs.q: Is an addition cheaper than remodeling the same square footage?
faqs.a: More per square foot than remodeling the same area, because you are buying structure before you buy anything you can see. Foundations, tie beams, roof tie-ins, impact-rated openings and added mechanical capacity are spent before a tile is chosen, and flood or design-review requirements can move the figure again. We do not publish a per-foot price, because the honest answer depends on the lot, the existing structure and the jurisdiction. You get a real range early, before you commit to drawings, and a fixed written scope before we commit to building.

faqs.q: Where does the calendar actually go on an addition?
faqs.a: Longer than the construction schedule implies, because the front end is where the calendar actually goes. Survey, design, structural engineering, association or design-board approval and municipal plan review all come first, each moving at its own pace. For a substantial addition, several months of that before ground breaks is normal, with construction running months beyond it. Counting from the first conversation to the day furniture arrives, a year is realistic for substantial work. The sequence is written down at estimate stage, so nobody spends a month wondering whose turn it is.

faqs.q: What approvals does adding square footage trigger?
faqs.a: Yes. Adding conditioned square footage is permitted work everywhere in Miami-Dade and Broward, and it draws more than a building review. Zoning looks at setbacks and lot coverage, structural review looks at sealed engineering, flood review applies wherever the property sits in a mapped zone, and a house on septic needs its system capacity reviewed before you add a bedroom, because the sizing tables are keyed to bedroom count. Historic and design-review boards enter earlier still. Unpermitted additions surface at appraisal, at closing or at insurance renewal, and cost more to legalize than to have built correctly.

faqs.q: Will the rest of the house have to come up to current code?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and that is worth learning before design rather than after. The addition itself is always built to current code. Whether the requirement reaches back into the existing house depends on what you open up, what the structure needs in order to carry new load, and, in a flood zone, on FEMA's substantial-improvement rule. Cross that threshold and the whole building has to comply. Whether the new wing is structurally connected to the old one matters there too. We run the analysis early, because it changes the design, not only the budget.

faqs.q: What can stop an addition, or shrink it?
faqs.a: Usually the lot rather than the house. Setbacks, easements, lot coverage and drainage set the buildable envelope, and a current survey shows less room than the yard suggests. After that: an association or design board unwilling to approve the massing, a required floor elevation higher than you pictured, a septic system with no capacity for another bedroom, or an engineer's report that makes going up cost more than going out. In a condominium, added area touches common elements: a vote before a build. None of these are fatal during feasibility. All of them are expensive after drawings.

faqs.q: What is daily life like while the house is open?
faqs.a: A PGX supervisor is there every working day, plus one project manager you can reach by name. Subcontractors work to our schedule and our written scope, and the trades are sequenced so inspections pass the first time instead of stacking up behind each other. The occupied half of the house stays dust-sealed and livable, finishes are protected, and the site is closed down cleanly each evening. PGX has been building here for more than twenty years, past 150 remodels and additions, every one of them permitted and inspected under Lic. CGC1539072.
